newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans protest against transport of nuclear waste.
newsitem.headline: Germans protest against transport of nuclear waste.

text.p: Thousands of German anti-nuclear demonstrators took to the streets on Saturday to protest against the transport of spent nuclear fuel to a storage depot in the north.

As protesters chanted slogans and waved banners, police geared up to launch the biggest security operation in Germany's post-war history to make sure activists do not threaten the safe arrival of shipment next week at the nearby Gorleben dump.
Over 10,000 demonstrators marched through the northern city of Lueneburg led by 100 tractors from the surrounding area and gathered in a park near the city centre for a rally.
Police were out in force to escort the march, but there were no reports of any trouble or arrests.
"We've had 20 years of resistance and nothing has happened. I hope this protest will show our strength," said one man carrying a child on his shoulders.

Four state environment ministers, all members of the opposition Greens, issued a joint statement calling on the government to store nuclear waste at the power stations which produced it rather than transporting it through Europe.

"The ever strengthening, justified protest of a wide section of the population against this transport to Gorleben must give politicians a chance to reflect on the current practice," the statement said.
Protests have heated up ahead of the shipment due to leave south Germany on Monday and arrive in Gorleben on Wednesday.
Suspected anti-nuclear activists have sabotaged rail lines, smashed windows of public buildings in Hamburg and daubed walls with anti-nuclear slogans.

In a sign of widespread local resistance, school children occupied two school halls in Hitzacker, a town near the Gorleben dump, to prevent them being used by police drafted into the area to protect the shipment.

The Lower Saxony state government has said around 30,000 police and border guards will be needed to protect the convoy and said the security operation would cost at least 66 million marks ($39 million).
Last year 19,000 police were needed to get a smaller load of nuclear waste past thousands of protesters and police fear a repeat of the violent clashes seen then.
Interior Minister Manfred Kanther told parliament on Thursday he would not shrink from a test of strength if it was forced on him by the activists.
But on Friday, as the nuclear waste convoy was assembled at Walheim in the south of the country, protests were mainly peaceful and police out-numbered demonstrators five to one.

Riot police carried away demonstrators sitting in front of the plant's gates and escorted the flatbed trucks carrying the three 112-tonne nuclear waste containers from a power plant past the demonstrators.
The containers from the nearby Neckarwestheim power plant were due to be put on flatbed rail cars together with shipments from France and Bavaria which also arrived on Friday.
Only a few small groups, including representatives from the environmentalist group Greenpeace, gathered at Walheim to protest on Saturday.
Greenpeace spokesman Sven Teske said they were only there as observers and said they would not increase the danger of the nuclear waste by interferring with it. ($ = 1.691 German Marks)
